sections.label: Section 1
sections.description: A conversation between two people in an everyday social context (e.g., booking a hotel, joining a club)
tips: You'll hear names, numbers, dates, and addresses — practice listening for spelling
The speaker often corrects themselves: 'Oh wait, it's actually...' — the SECOND answer is correct
Read the form BEFORE the audio starts — predict what kind of answer you need
Listen for signal words: 'that's', 'it's', 'the address is', 'my name is'

sections.label: Section 2
sections.description: A monologue in an everyday social context (e.g., a tour guide, a public announcement)
tips: One speaker only — harder to follow because there are no conversational cues
For map questions: orient yourself FIRST — find North, the entrance, landmarks
The speaker may describe things in a different order than the questions
Listen for direction words: 'opposite', 'next to', 'beyond', 'on your left'

sections.label: Section 3
sections.description: A discussion between 2-4 people in an educational context (e.g., students discussing an assignment)
tips: Multiple speakers — identify WHO is saying WHAT
Academic vocabulary is common — study topic-specific terms
One speaker may agree, disagree, or modify another's point — listen for the FINAL decision
Distractors: a speaker mentions an option but then rejects it — listen for the conclusion

sections.label: Section 4
sections.description: An academic lecture or talk on a general academic topic
tips: No pause in the middle — you must keep up for ~5 minutes straight
Read ALL questions before the audio — you won't get a second chance
The lecture follows a logical structure — use this to anticipate what comes next
Technical terms are often defined: 'This is known as...', 'What we call...'

generalStrategies.label: Predict Before You Listen
generalStrategies.description: Use the time before each section to read questions and predict answers
steps: Read the questions and underline key words
Predict the type of answer: name? number? place? adjective?
For gap-fills: check what comes before and after the gap — what part of speech fits?
For multiple choice: read ALL options — eliminate ones that seem unlikely

generalStrategies.label: Spelling & Numbers Mastery
generalStrategies.description: Section 1 almost always tests spelling and numbers — practise these daily
steps: Know the NATO alphabet for tricky letters: B/D, M/N, F/S, P/B
Double letters: 'double L', 'double T' — listen for the word 'double'
Phone numbers are usually read in groups: '07-700-554-238'
Dates: '14th of March' or 'March the 14th' — both are common
Money: 'fifty pounds' = £50, 'fifteen' vs 'fifty' — listen to the ending (-een vs -ty)
Addresses: house number + street name. Listen for 'Road', 'Street', 'Avenue', 'Lane', 'Drive'

generalStrategies.label: Spotting Distractors
generalStrategies.description: The test deliberately includes wrong answers to mislead you
steps: A speaker says one thing then corrects it: 'Tuesday... no, sorry, Wednesday' — answer is Wednesday
One speaker suggests something, another disagrees: follow the AGREED conclusion
An option is mentioned but in a DIFFERENT context than the question asks about
Extreme language ('always', 'never', 'all') is usually wrong in multiple choice
The answer usually paraphrases the question — if you hear the exact same words, be suspicious

generalStrategies.label: Note-Taking Method
generalStrategies.description: Quick notation system for the listening test
steps: Use abbreviations: w/ (with), b/c (because), govt (government), → (leads to)
Write only KEY words — not full sentences
Draw arrows to connect related ideas
Use ? for uncertain answers — come back to them
Write answers on the question paper first, then transfer to the answer sheet at the end (you get 10 minutes)

commonMistakes.fix: If you miss an answer, move on immediately. Don't dwell — you'll miss the next one too.
Spelling must be correct. Practise common IELTS words: accommodation, environment, government, necessary.
If the limit is 'ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER', don't write two words. Articles (a/the) count.
Read the instruction EVERY time. Different question sets can have different word limits.
Always guess — there's no penalty for wrong answers. Write something logical.
Practise minimal pairs: fifteen/fifty, Monday/Sunday, B/P, G/J, I/E.
Speakers often self-correct. The FINAL answer they give is the correct one.
You get 10 minutes to transfer. Use them carefully. Check spelling and word limits.

practiceExercises.label: Spelling Drill
practiceExercises.description: Common IELTS words that are frequently misspelled

pairs.tip: thirTEEN (stress on -teen) vs THIRty (stress on first syllable)
